headline: Autonomous AI agent earns $500 by hunting online bounties, filtering scams
summary: A new AI agent autonomously scans 232+ listings, filters scams, generates deliverables, and proposes work, earning $500 on its first bounty. It requires minimal human oversight for approval.
details: An AI agent was tasked with finding paid online work, building deliverables, and earning money autonomously. In its first 24 hours, it scanned over 232 listings across multiple platforms. The agent successfully filtered out scams and ghost sponsors, demonstrating its ability to navigate complex online marketplaces.

The agent identified a $500 bounty requiring a Solana ecosystem report. It gathered live data from CoinGecko, DeFiLlama, and Solana RPC, then used a local LLM to generate a full markdown analysis and an interactive dashboard. This comprehensive deliverable was prepared with minimal human intervention.

Human effort was reduced to reviewing the generated work, clicking an 'approve' command, and pasting the submission. This highlights the agent's efficiency in automating the entire workflow from job discovery to deliverable creation, pending final human oversight.

The creator noted that the market for AI-doable bounties is thin, with only 2-5 suitable listings out of 232 after filtering. The agent successfully identified and avoided 'ghost sponsors' like 'Aeonian Trade,' which sought free work without legitimate payment.

A crucial element is the learning loop, where confirmed payments feed back into the agent's priority engine to optimize future searches. This iterative improvement ensures the agent becomes more effective over time in identifying profitable opportunities.

The project emphasizes the necessity of a 'human-in-the-loop' for financial transactions. While the AI agent handles discovery and building, human review and submission are essential to prevent scams and ensure ethical operation.

headline_marked: [[Shopify's agent-commerce category filter doesn't filter]]. We checked 190 stores.
headline: Shopify's agent-commerce category filter doesn't filter. We checked 190 stores.
summary: A recent study of 190 Shopify stores found that the agent-commerce category filter, part of the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), fails to narrow product searches by category despite its declared schema. This means AI shopping agents cannot effectively filter
details: Since 2026, every Shopify storefront includes an agent-commerce endpoint at /api/ucp/mcp, speaking the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) over JSON-RPC. Its search_catalog tool allows AI shopping agents to retrieve structured product data, including taxonomy categories.

The search_catalog tool's schema declares catalog.filters.categories, an array of strings for category filtering, alongside working price filters. This suggests agents should be able to request specific product categories.

Researchers deterministically sampled 200 Shopify storefronts from a corpus of 10,099. On September 2, 2026, each store received five calls, requesting 10 products with various filter combinations, including category filters.

Out of 190 readable stores, 177 returned products with taxonomy categories. However, the category filter consistently failed to narrow results, returning the same products regardless of the category specified.

A control test using the price.max filter in the same calls confirmed that the requests were correctly formed and that other filters functioned as expected, isolating the issue specifically to the category filter.
This does not mean uncategorized products are invisible to agents; rather, the filter simply doesn't apply any exclusion logic. A blank category field does not prevent products from being returned.
The finding confirms that, on the 190 stores tested, an agent cannot narrow a catalog search by category today, despite the Universal Commerce Protocol's declared schema.

This is not a criticism of Shopify but highlights that for a young protocol like UCP, the schema may precede full behavioral implementation. The key lesson is to test endpoint behavior rather than solely relying on documentation.
All 190 readings, including domain, query, product counts for each call, and the verdict, are publicly available in filter-survey.csv for full reproducibility.
